subject: How can I optimize my stan model

messages.author: c206abeed36f358b
messages.subject: How can I optimize my stan model
parts:
Hello everyone,

I have a Stan model which runs much slower than its equivalent JAGS model. I've tried different ways but wan't able to speed it up. I'd appreciate any advice on optimizing the model. Thanks!

Here is the Stan model:

data {
  int<lower=0> Ny;
  int<lower=0> NR;
  int<lower=0> NQ;
  int<lower=1, upper=NR> R[Ny];
  int<lower=1, upper=NQ> Q[Ny];
  real y[Ny];
}
parameters {
  real b0;
  real bR[NR];
  real bQ[NQ];
  real<lower=0,upper=10> sy;
  real<lower=0> sR;
  real<lower=0> sQ[NQ];
}
transformed parameters {
  real mu[Ny];
  for (i in 1 : Ny) 
    mu[i] <- b0 + bR[R[i]] + bQ[Q[i]];
}
model {
  sR ~ gamma(1.01005, 0.1005);
  sQ ~ gamma(1.01005, 0.1005);
  b0 ~ normal(0, 33);
  bR ~ normal(0.0, sR);
  bQ ~ normal(0.0, sQ);
  y ~ normal(mu, sy);
}

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How can I optimize my stan model
parts:
Have you double-checked the use of distributions in Stan vs. JAGS? I know there are some differences in parameterization.

The normal distribution is parameterized by the mean and standard deviation in Stan. In JAGS, it is mean and precision (1 / variance, or 1 / sd^2).


On first glance, there doesn't seem to be any glaring issues with the model. Do the posterior distributions look the same as in JAGS? Have you looked at effective sample size / time?


Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How can I optimize my stan model
parts:
Thanks Daniel. I noticed the parameterization differences between Stan and JAGS (see JAGS model below). 
Where should I look for effective sample size / time? I just ran rjags and rstan with the same input data, using their default setting (1000 iterations for rjags and 2000 iterations for rstan). The posterior means looks similar to me.

The equivalent JAGS model:
models$nsig_rRFX_qFFX$params = c("b0", "bR", "bQ")
models$nsig_rRFX_qFFX$modelStr = "
model {
## Likelihoods ##
for (i in 1:Ny) {
  # data are sum of two INDEPENDENT factors
  y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau_y)
  mu[i] <- b0 + bR[R[i]] + bQ[Q[i]]
}
tau_y <- 1/pow(sigma_y, 2) # jags dnorm takes precision, not variance
sigma_y ~ dunif(0,10)      # y values are assumed to be standardized

## Linear factor priors ##
b0 ~ dnorm(0,0.001)

# bR prior
for (j in 1:NR) {
  bR[j] ~ dnorm(0.0, tau_bR)
}
tau_bR <- 1/pow(sigma_bR, 2)
sigma_bR ~ dgamma(1.01005,0.1005) # mean:10.05, var:100.00, mode:0.10

# bQ prior
for (k in 1:NQ) {
  bQ[k] ~ dnorm(0.0, tau_bQ[k])
  tau_bQ[k] <- 1/pow(s2[k], 2)
  s2[k] ~ dgamma(1.01005, 0.1005) # mean: 10.05, var: 100.00, mode: 0.10
}
}"

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How can I optimize my stan model
parts:
Hi, I have three thoughts.

1.  Why is sQ defined as an array rather than a scalar?  Do you really have a different variance parameter for each bQ?  This is an unusual model.

2.  It could run faster, maybe, if you code the arrays as vectors.

3.  This looks like a basic multilevel model so indeed we would not want it running much slower in Stan than in Jags.  One thing you could do is the Matt trick, which should help if the hierarchical variance parameters are close to 0.

You reparameterize like this:

mu[i] <- b0 + sR*bR[R[i]] + sQ*bQ[Q[i]];

and, later on:

bR ~ normal (0,1)
bQ ~ normal (0,1)

This particular separation can help.  (We have a paper on it which unfortunately is not yet released.)

Beyond this, perhaps there is something in the way the code works below that is slow for some reason in Stan.  I'm not sure why that would be, but the people closer to the Stan development might have an idea.

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How can I optimize my stan model
parts:
Are you comparing time per iteration or time per effective
sample? We only care about the latter.

More below.

On 11/27/13, 3:11 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, I have three thoughts.
>
> 1. Why is sQ defined as an array rather than a scalar? Do you really have a different variance parameter for each bQ?
> This is an unusual model.
>
> 2. It could run faster, maybe, if you code the arrays as vectors.

That won't be any faster. I wrote a new chapter in the manual
that explains the efficiency issues of arrays vs. vectors as well
as when you need to use vectors (matrix algebra).

> 3. This looks like a basic multilevel model so indeed we would not want it running much slower in Stan than in Jags.
> One thing you could do is the Matt trick, which should help if the hierarchical variance parameters are close to 0.
>
> You reparameterize like this:
>
> mu[i] <- b0 + sR*bR[R[i]] + sQ*bQ[Q[i]];
>
> and, later on:
>
> bR ~ normal (0,1)
> bQ ~ normal (0,1)
>
> This particular separation can help. (We have a paper on it which unfortunately is not yet released.)

There's also the gamma reparameterization. Don't know if
that's relevant because I barely understand it or its geometric
implications.

> Beyond this, perhaps there is something in the way the code works below that is slow for some reason in Stan. I'm not
> sure why that would be, but the people closer to the Stan development might have an idea.

The model's about as tight as it can be in terms of code.

- Bob

On Wednesday, November 27, 2013 12:11:28 PM UTC-8, Andrew Gelman wrote:

Hi, I have three thoughts.

1.  Why is sQ defined as an array rather than a scalar?  Do you really have a different variance parameter for each bQ?  This is an unusual model.

Yes, each bQ has different variance. An example is, suppose y is people's evaluations on some products, and Q is the the product IDs. Then the evaluation variances on different products are different.
2.  It could run faster, maybe, if you code the arrays as vectors.
I tried this, unfortunately it is about the same.

3.  This looks like a basic multilevel model so indeed we would not want it running much slower in Stan than in Jags.  One thing you could do is the Matt trick, which should help if the hierarchical variance parameters are close to 0.

You reparameterize like this:

mu[i] <- b0 + sR*bR[R[i]] + sQ*bQ[Q[i]];

and, later on:

bR ~ normal (0,1)
bQ ~ normal (0,1)

This particular separation can help.  (We have a paper on it which unfortunately is not yet released.)
 
Beyond this, perhaps there is something in the way the code works below that is slow for some reason in Stan.  I'm not sure why that would be, but the people closer to the Stan development might have an idea.

A
